title: Beer vs Liquor Hangover: Which Is Worse? What the Science Says
excerpt: Does beer give you a worse hangover than liquor? What the research shows about alcohol amount, congeners, clear vs dark spirits, carbonation, and pace.
metaDescription: Does beer give you a worse hangover than liquor? What research says about alcohol amount, congeners, clear vs dark liquor, and how to pick your drinks.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** gram for gram of alcohol, beer does not give you a worse hangover than liquor. The single biggest driver of how bad you feel the next morning is how much alcohol you drank and how fast, not whether it came in a pint glass or a shot glass. Where the type of drink does matter, it tends to work against dark liquors (bourbon, brandy, dark rum), not beer, because they carry more of the by-products called congeners. So why do so many people swear beer hangovers are worse? Usually because beer nights involve more total alcohol than they realize, spread over more hours, with more bloating and broken sleep. This guide walks through what the research actually shows, why beer hangovers can *feel* different, and how to pick and pace your drinks if you want a better morning.

**The quick rules:** Count standard drinks, not glasses. A strong craft beer can hold two standard drinks or more. If you drink liquor, clear spirits like vodka and gin tend to produce slightly milder hangovers than dark ones at the same dose, but the difference is small compared with drinking less. The order you drink things in ("beer before liquor") doesn't change much on its own. Alternate with water, eat beforehand, and slow down.

> **When to see a doctor or get help.** A normal hangover is miserable but passes within about a day. **Call 911 or get emergency care if someone** is confused or hard to wake, is vomiting repeatedly and can't keep water down, has slow or irregular breathing, has seizures, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a bad hangover, and the person should not be left to "sleep it off." **See a doctor soon if** you get vomiting that lasts more than a day, blood in vomit or stools, chest pain, a severe headache unlike your usual ones, or yellowing of the skin or eyes. If you notice shaking, sweating, anxiety or a racing heart that only settles when you drink again, mention it to a doctor. Those can be early withdrawal signals and are worth taking seriously, even for people who think of themselves as social drinkers.

## Does Beer Give You a Worse Hangover Than Liquor?

Not when you compare the same amount of alcohol. Hangover researchers have been fairly consistent on this: the main predictor of hangover severity is the total amount of alcohol consumed and how high your blood alcohol got. Researchers in the Alcohol Hangover Research Group, a network of scientists who study hangovers, have repeatedly reported that the dose of alcohol explains far more of the next-day misery than the type of drink.

The best direct evidence on beer comes from a 2019 study in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* by Jöran Köchling and colleagues at Witten/Herdecke University in Germany. They had about 90 young adult volunteers drink beer, wine, or both in a controlled setting, then come back a week later and do it again in a different arrangement. The study was designed to test the "beer before wine" saying, and it found that the order made no meaningful difference. What predicted a worse hangover was how drunk people felt and whether they vomited. In other words, more alcohol, worse morning.

So if your beer nights tend to leave you wrecked and your liquor nights don't, the drink itself is rarely the main reason. The pattern of drinking almost always is.

### Why it often feels like beer is worse

A few very ordinary things make beer nights hit harder for many people:

- **Beer nights are often longer.** People tend to settle in with beer for an evening at a bar, a game, or a barbecue. Six hours of steady beers adds up, even if each one feels light.
- **Strong beers are stronger than they look.** A standard US beer is around 5% alcohol in a 12-ounce can. Many IPAs and stouts run 7 to 10%, often poured in 16-ounce pints. One of those can easily equal two standard drinks.
- **It's harder to count.** "A few beers" is vague in a way that "four shots" is not. People who would never take eight shots will cheerfully have eight beers.
- **Volume and fullness.** Beer means a lot of liquid and gas. That can mean bloating, a sour stomach and repeated trips to the bathroom at night, which chip away at sleep quality.

None of that is because beer is a more toxic form of alcohol. It's because the beer night delivered more alcohol, more slowly noticed, alongside more stomach upset.

## How Much Alcohol Is Actually in Your Drink?

This is the most useful thing to get right. In the US, one standard drink contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's roughly:

| Drink | Typical serving | Approximate standard drinks |
|---|---|---|
| Regular beer (about 5%) | 12 oz can or bottle | 1 |
| Light beer (about 4%) | 12 oz can | about 0.8 |
| Craft IPA (about 7%) | 16 oz pint | about 1.9 |
| Double IPA or imperial stout (about 9 to 10%) | 16 oz pint | about 2.5 to 2.7 |
| Wine (about 12%) | 5 oz glass | 1 |
| Spirits (about 40%, 80 proof) | 1.5 oz shot | 1 |
| Mixed drink or cocktail | varies | often 1.5 to 3 |

The point of this table is that "beer" and "liquor" aren't fixed amounts. A pint of double IPA can carry more alcohol than a well-poured vodka soda, and a long cocktail with several spirits can carry more than both. Our [standard drink guide](/never-hungover/what-is-a-standard-drink) goes through how to work out what's in your glass.

When people say "beer gives me a worse hangover than liquor," it's worth honestly comparing the standard drinks on each kind of night. Most of the time, the beer night wins on total alcohol.

## What Does Differ Between Beer and Liquor

The amount of alcohol is the big lever, but it isn't the only one. A few real differences between drinks can nudge a hangover in one direction or the other.

### Congeners: the by-products that come along for the ride

Congeners are compounds other than ethanol (drinking alcohol) that form during fermentation and aging. They include methanol, other "fusel" alcohols, acetaldehyde, esters and tannins. They contribute to flavor and color, and some of them seem to make hangovers worse.

As a rough rule, darker and more aged drinks carry more congeners. Bourbon, brandy, whiskey, dark rum and red wine sit at the high end. Vodka, gin and white rum sit at the low end. Beer is in the middle, depending on style. It contains some fusel alcohols and other fermentation by-products, but not usually at the levels found in brandy or bourbon.

The research here is real but modest:

- A small study from the 1970s by Pawan found that bourbon produced more hangover symptoms than the same dose of vodka.
- A 2010 study by Damaris Rohsenow and colleagues, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research*, gave volunteers either bourbon or vodka to reach the same fairly high blood alcohol level. Bourbon produced somewhat worse self-reported hangovers than vodka. However, next-day performance on attention and reaction-time tests was impaired about equally by both. The alcohol itself did most of the damage.

So congeners appear to add a bit on top. They don't change the basic math. Our guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains which drinks carry the most and why.

### Clear liquor vs dark liquor

If you drink spirits and want the milder option, clear liquors like vodka and gin tend to produce slightly lighter hangovers than dark ones like bourbon, brandy or dark rum at the same dose. The congener studies above are the reason. It's a real effect, but a small one. Four vodka sodas will still leave you worse off than two bourbons.

Two practical notes:

- **Clear doesn't mean "safe."** Vodka is easy to drink fast and easy to hide in sweet mixers. That makes it easy to overdo.
- **Cheap vs expensive is murkier.** You'll often hear that cheap vodka causes worse hangovers. There's no good evidence that price on its own predicts hangover severity. Distillation quality affects congener levels, and some cheaper spirits may carry more, but bottle price is a poor guide.

### Where beer sits on congeners

Beer is not a high-congener drink compared with dark spirits, but it isn't a clean one either. Darker, stronger and more heavily hopped beers tend to carry more flavor compounds and fusel alcohols than light lagers. If you notice that certain beer styles leave you worse off, that may be part of it, though the higher alcohol in those styles is usually the bigger factor. Our [beer hangover guide](/never-hungover/beer-hangover) goes deeper on beer specifically.

### Carbonation and speed of absorption

Bubbles may help alcohol get into your blood faster. Some small studies have found that alcohol mixed with carbonated water was absorbed faster than the same alcohol mixed with still water or drunk neat, though not every person in those studies responded the same way. That's one reason champagne and vodka-soda can seem to "hit" quickly.

Beer is carbonated, but it's also dilute. Liquor mixed with soda or tonic is carbonated and usually more concentrated. So carbonation doesn't clearly favor either side. What matters more is how quickly you drink.

### Concentration and pace

Liquor is concentrated. A shot can be gone in a second, and a strong cocktail can be finished in a few minutes. That can push your blood alcohol up quickly, which is linked to worse impairment and, for many people, worse hangovers. Beer's sheer volume naturally slows some drinkers down.

This works in both directions. Shots and strong cocktails can produce a sharp spike. Beer can produce a long, slow climb to the same or higher total. Neither is kind to you if the total is high.

### Fluid and dehydration

Alcohol makes you urinate more by suppressing a hormone called vasopressin, which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. Beer brings a lot of water with it, so you might expect it to dehydrate you less. There's some support for that idea at the low-alcohol end. Studies by Hobson and Maughan in the UK found that lower-alcohol beer was handled more like a normal drink by the body, while stronger beer increased urine output. But at normal beer strength over a long night, you'll still lose plenty of fluid, and your sleep will be broken by bathroom trips.

Dehydration is only one part of a hangover anyway. Researchers now think inflammation, poor sleep, acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product of alcohol breakdown) and the body's immune response all play a role. Drinking water helps you feel better, but it doesn't erase the other parts.

### Sugar and mixers

Sweet cocktails, liqueurs and sugary mixers make alcohol easier to drink quickly and harder to taste. There's no good evidence that sugar itself causes a worse hangover, but it can mask how much alcohol you're getting. Diet mixers have a separate wrinkle: a small study found that alcohol mixed with diet soda produced higher breath alcohol readings than the same alcohol mixed with regular soda, likely because sugar slows stomach emptying. That doesn't mean sugar is protective. It just means mixers change how fast the alcohol arrives.

## What About Mixing Beer and Liquor?

The famous rhyme says "beer before liquor, never been sicker; liquor before beer, you're in the clear." The order on its own doesn't seem to matter much. The 2019 German study tested this directly with beer and wine and found no meaningful difference between the orders. The best explanation for the rhyme is behavioral: if you start a night with beer and move on to shots, you're often already tipsy when the strong drinks arrive, which makes it easier to drink too much, too fast.

Mixing different drinks in one night isn't uniquely toxic either. What usually happens is that switching drinks makes it harder to keep count. You lose track of the total, and the total is what drives the hangover. If you want the full breakdown of the rhyme and the study behind it, see [beer before liquor: myth or fact](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth).

## Is Beer or Liquor Better for Avoiding a Hangover?

If you're choosing a drink with the morning in mind, here's an honest ranking of what matters most, roughly from biggest to smallest effect:

1. **Total alcohol.** Fewer standard drinks is by far the strongest factor.
2. **Pace.** Spreading drinks out keeps your blood alcohol lower than drinking the same amount quickly.
3. **Food.** Eating a real meal before drinking slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream.
4. **Sleep.** Alcohol wrecks sleep quality, and a short, broken night makes everything worse.
5. **Drink type.** Lower-congener drinks like vodka, gin, light beer and white wine tend to be a little gentler than bourbon, brandy, dark rum and red wine at the same dose.

So the best "hangover-friendly" choice isn't beer or liquor as a category. It's a drink that's easy to count and easy to pace. For some people that's a light beer they sip slowly. For others it's a single measured vodka soda followed by water. Pick whichever helps *you* drink less without noticing.

### If you're drinking beer

- **Check the ABV.** Choose sessionable or light styles (around 4 to 5%) over 8% IPAs if you plan to have several.
- **Mind the pour.** A 16-ounce pint is a third bigger than a 12-ounce can.
- **Alternate.** A glass of water between beers slows you down and cuts how much alcohol you drink overall.
- **Eat.** Beer drinking often happens alongside food anyway, which helps.

### If you're drinking liquor

- **Use a measure.** Free-poured drinks at home are often double a standard shot.
- **Go clear if you want a small edge.** Vodka, gin and white rum carry fewer congeners than bourbon or brandy.
- **Skip the shot rounds.** Shots spike blood alcohol fastest.
- **Watch the mixers.** Sweet mixers hide the taste of alcohol, so it's easy to drink faster than you mean to.

## Does Beer Cause Different Hangover Symptoms Than Liquor?

There's no reliable research showing that beer and liquor produce distinct sets of symptoms. A hangover is a hangover: headache, fatigue, thirst, nausea, poor concentration, low mood and sensitivity to light and sound.

That said, people do often describe beer hangovers a little differently, and the reasons make sense:

- **More bloating and stomach upset** from carbonation and sheer volume.
- **More broken sleep** from getting up to use the bathroom.
- **More of a dull, heavy, sluggish feeling** after a long session, compared with the sharper, more nauseous feeling some people get after shots.

Some people also report headaches with specific beers, which can come down to alcohol strength, congeners, or personal sensitivities. A small number of people react to things like gluten, yeast or histamine in certain drinks. If you consistently get symptoms like flushing, hives, a stuffy nose or a pounding headache after just one drink, that's worth mentioning to a doctor. It may be an intolerance rather than a hangover. Our guides on [beer headaches](/never-hungover/beer-headache) and the [general symptoms of a hangover](/never-hungover/hangover-symptoms) cover these in more detail.

## Wine, Beer and Liquor Side by Side

Wine often gets pulled into this comparison, so here's a quick summary:

| Factor | Beer | Wine | Liquor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alcohol per typical serving | about 1 standard drink (more for strong craft beer) | about 1 standard drink per 5 oz | about 1 standard drink per shot; cocktails often more |
| Congeners | moderate, varies by style | moderate (white) to high (red) | low (clear) to high (dark) |
| Volume of liquid | high | moderate | low (unless mixed) |
| Typical pace | slow and steady over a long session | moderate | can be very fast (shots) |
| Common next-day complaint | bloating, broken sleep, heavy fatigue | headache, especially with red wine | nausea, sharper hangover after shots |

None of these differences beat the amount of alcohol. They just shape the details. If you're curious about the "wine drunk feels different from beer drunk" idea, we cover it in [wine drunk vs beer drunk](/never-hungover/wine-drunk-vs-beer-drunk).

## What Actually Reduces a Hangover, Whatever You Drink

There is no drink choice that removes the hangover from a heavy night. The basics with the best support are dull but effective:

- **Drink less, or drink slower.** Every standard drink you skip makes a difference.
- **Eat a proper meal first.** Food in your stomach slows absorption.
- **Alternate with water.** It helps with thirst and cuts down how much alcohol you drink.
- **Protect your sleep.** Stop drinking a few hours before bed if you can.
- **Avoid painkillers "just in case" before bed.** Deal with a headache in the morning, after you've eaten. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) in particular is hard on the liver alongside alcohol.

Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through each of these and the evidence behind them.

### Where DHM fits

Some people also try supplements. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It's promising, but there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in people, and it doesn't change how much alcohol is in your drink. If you want to try it alongside the basics, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. No supplement makes heavy drinking safe.

## The Bottom Line

- At the same amount of alcohol, beer doesn't give you a worse hangover than liquor.
- The amount of alcohol and how fast you drink it matter far more than the drink type.
- Beer nights often feel worse because they quietly involve more alcohol, more liquid, more bloating and more broken sleep.
- Dark liquors like bourbon and brandy tend to cause slightly worse hangovers than clear ones like vodka and gin, because of congeners. The effect is real but small.
- The order you drink beer and liquor in doesn't matter much on its own. Losing count does.
- Pick the drink that helps you count and pace, eat first, alternate with water, and know the signs of alcohol poisoning.

For the bigger picture, our [ranking of drinks by hangover risk](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) puts every major drink type side by side, and our guide to [congeners](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains the by-products behind the differences. If you're choosing between spirits, our [vodka vs tequila](/never-hungover/vodka-vs-tequila-hangover) comparison goes a level deeper.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does beer give you a worse hangover than liquor?**

Not when you compare the same amount of alcohol. Hangover severity is driven mainly by how much alcohol you drink and how fast. Beer nights often feel worse because they tend to involve more total alcohol over a longer session, plus more bloating and broken sleep. If anything, dark liquors like bourbon and brandy are linked to slightly worse hangovers than beer because they carry more congeners.

**Is beer or liquor worse for a hangover?**

Neither is worse as a category. A pint of 9% craft beer can hold more alcohol than a single vodka soda, and a round of shots can spike your blood alcohol faster than a slow beer. Compare standard drinks, not glasses. Among liquors, clear spirits tend to be slightly gentler than dark ones at the same dose.

**Why do I get worse hangovers from beer?**

The most common reasons are that beer nights last longer, strong craft beers carry more alcohol than people expect, and it's easier to lose count of beers than shots. Beer's volume and carbonation can also cause bloating and more bathroom trips that break up your sleep. Less often, some people react to specific ingredients in certain beers, which is worth raising with a doctor if it happens after even one drink.

**Is clear liquor better for hangovers than dark liquor?**

Slightly, at the same dose. Studies comparing bourbon and vodka found that bourbon produced somewhat worse self-reported hangovers, likely because of its higher congener content. But next-day performance was impaired about equally by both, so the alcohol itself does most of the damage. Drinking less matters far more than choosing vodka over whiskey.

**Does mixing beer and liquor make a hangover worse?**

Not by itself. A 2019 controlled study found that the order of beer and wine didn't change hangover severity. Mixing drinks mostly makes it harder to keep track of how much you've had, and the total amount is what drives the hangover.

**Which alcohol gives the least hangover?**

Lower-congener drinks such as vodka, gin, light beer and white wine tend to produce slightly milder hangovers than bourbon, brandy, dark rum and red wine at the same dose. The difference is small. The drink that gives you the least hangover is usually the one you drink the least of, slowly, with food.

**Does carbonation in beer make you drunk faster?**

Carbonation may speed up how fast alcohol is absorbed. Some small studies found faster absorption when alcohol was mixed with carbonated water, though results varied between people. Beer is carbonated but dilute, while spirits with soda are carbonated and more concentrated, so carbonation alone doesn't make beer worse than liquor.

**When is a hangover a reason to see a doctor?**

Get emergency help if someone is confused or hard to wake, keeps vomiting and can't hold down water, has slow or irregular breathing, has seizures, or has cold, pale or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning. See a doctor if vomiting lasts more than a day, you notice blood in vomit or stools, you have chest pain or an unusually severe headache, or you get shaking and sweating that only ease when you drink again.
